item.title: Product Thinking (4): Self-Healing Systems — Teaching Machines to Fix Themselves
item.description:
The Bug That Fixed Itself#

One morning in late May 2026, I woke up to a DingTalk notification from my research agent system:

“self_heal Rule 37 triggered: restarted research-pipeline after 3 consecutive OOM kills. Root cause: scanner thread retained full PDF buffers across iterations. Applied patch: explicit del after extraction. Validation: 45 minutes post-patch, RSS stable at 1.2 GB (was 2.4 GB pre-patch).”

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (7): Turn Every Scar Into a Rule
item.description:
Every lesson in this series started the same way: something broke, I diagnosed it, I fixed it. That’s the normal loop, and most people stop there. This final note is about the step after the fix — the one that turns a private scar into a permanent property of the system, so nobody (including future-you) has to bleed for it twice.

I think of it as apprenticeship in reverse. A master teaches an apprentice not just what to do but how to judge when to do it. When you fix something, you’ve just learned a judgment. The question is: can you teach that judgment to the system, so the system makes the right call next time without you?

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (6): Re-Verify the Old Fixes Every Round
item.description: If you run a system in a continuous improvement loop — round after round of “find something to make better, change it, verify, repeat” — you eventually hit a specific, demoralizing failure: a change in round 20 quietly re-breaks something you carefully fixed in round 8. Everyone was watching the new change. Nobody was watching the old guarantee. And because the old fix had been working for twelve rounds, it wasn’t on anyone’s mind.

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (5): Autonomy That Won't Nuke the Wrong Thing
item.description:
The previous four notes were about verification — proving work happened. This one is about the opposite risk: letting an agent take destructive action on its own, and having it confidently destroy the wrong thing.

Autonomy is the entire reason to build agents. An agent that has to ask permission for every action isn’t automation, it’s a slow human with extra steps. But the failure mode of autonomy is uniquely bad: a human who deletes the wrong row usually notices and stops; an agent executing a plan will happily delete the wrong row, then the next, then the next, at machine speed and with total confidence.

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (4): Deployed Is Not Executed
item.description:
There’s a specific flavor of self-deception that shows up once your changes get big enough to have plumbing. You write a feature. You deploy it. The deploy succeeds. You mark it done. And it never runs — not because it’s broken, but because nothing actually calls it on the path you care about.

I’ve shipped this bug enough times that I now treat “deployed” and “working” as unrelated facts until proven otherwise. This note is about the two ways the gap opens, and how to close each.

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (3): Charge Before You Produce
item.description:
An agent that only reads is easy to make reliable — worst case, you re-run it. An agent that spends — money, quota, a rate-limited API budget — or that mutates shared state is where ordering bugs live. This note is about a handful of sequencing rules that decide whether a crash at the worst possible instant costs you money or leaves you clean.

None of these are clever. They’re all just “be paranoid in the right order.”

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (2): Safety Nets Beat Flaky Observers
item.description:
The first note argued that the build is the only acceptance gate. This one is about what happens when the observer — the thing that’s supposed to tell you a piece of work landed — is itself unreliable. Because sometimes the code is correct and the trigger that’s supposed to activate it just… doesn’t fire.

I lost a genuinely embarrassing amount of time to a bug in this family, so this note is mostly a scar.

item.title: Field Notes on Reliable Agents (1): The Build Is the Only Gate
item.description:
Last month a three-agent run left me with a repo that would not compile, and every agent in it had reported success. That contradiction is the whole subject of this note.

The setup was ordinary. A parent agent split a refactor into three tasks and handed each to a child. Child A moved a shared type into a new module. Child B renamed a function that type referenced. Child C deleted a config field that, three files away, was still read. Each child ran tsc --noEmit on the files it had touched, saw no errors, and returned {"status": "done"}. The parent collected three “done"s and moved on.
